title: The Company You Keep
excerpt: Proverbs says we become like the people we walk with. Friends who sharpen us, tell us the truth, and the friend who sticks closer than a brother.

blocks.text: Try something for a moment. Think of the five people you spend the most time with, or talk to the most. Not the people you wish you saw more, but the ones who actually fill your days, your texts, your group chats.
Got them?

Now ask a slightly uncomfortable question. Are you becoming more like Christ around those people, or less? Do you leave their company braver or smaller? More honest or more guarded? More hopeful or more cynical?

Most of us never ask this. We think of friendship as something that happens *to* us, a matter of who we click with, who lives nearby, who we ended up sitting next to. But Proverbs sees it differently. It treats the people we walk with as one of the most powerful forces shaping the person we become, and it says so with surprising bluntness.
You Become Who You Walk With

verses: Walk with the wise and become wise, for a companion of fools suffers harm.

blocks.text: Notice the verb. It doesn't say *listen to* the wise. It says *walk with* them. Wisdom, like a lot of things, is caught more than taught. You absorb it through proximity: the way someone handles a hard week, what they laugh at, what they refuse to say, how they treat the waiter. You can't help picking up the habits, attitudes, and assumptions of the people closest to you, and usually you don't notice it happening.

That cuts both ways. Proverbs gives a pointed warning elsewhere: "Do not make friends with a hot-tempered person, do not associate with one easily angered, or you may learn their ways and get yourself ensnared" (22:24–25). *You may learn their ways.* Not decide to, just learn. Slowly, quietly, without ever making a decision.

None of this is about being a snob or cutting off everyone who's struggling. Jesus was famously called "a friend of tax collectors and sinners" (Luke 7:34), and He loved them without being shaped by them. But He did that from a place of deep rootedness, and He still went off alone to pray. The question isn't "should I spend time with imperfect people?" (everyone is). It's "who is shaping me, and in which direction?"
Friction Is the Point
Here's a verse many of us know without realizing how strange it is:

verses: As iron sharpens iron, so one person sharpens another.

blocks.text: Think about what that image actually involves. Sharpening iron means scraping iron against iron. Sparks fly. There's noise, pressure, friction. Nobody gets sharper by being politely left alone.

Which is a bit inconvenient, because a lot of us want friendships that never rub. We want agreeable company, people who nod along, validate us, and never push back. But a friend who never challenges you isn't sharpening anything. They're just keeping you comfortable. And comfort, as lovely as it feels, is rarely where growth happens.

Think of Jonathan and David. David was on the run, hunted by a jealous king, exhausted and afraid. And Scripture says that Jonathan "went to David... and helped him find strength in God" (1 Samuel 23:16). Look at what he did. He didn't just say "everything will be fine." He pointed David back to God. That's iron sharpening iron. A real friend makes you better at trusting God, not just feel better about your circumstances.
The Friend Who Tells You the Truth
Then there's this verse, which might be the most countercultural line in the whole book on friendship:

verses: Wounds from a friend can be trusted, but an enemy multiplies kisses.

blocks.text: Read that again slowly. A friend can wound you, and you can still trust them. And someone who flatters you constantly, who showers you with praise and agreement and never says anything difficult, might actually be doing you harm.

That's a hard thing to hear, especially in a world that tends to confuse *support* with *constant affirmation.* But think about the people in your life whose opinion has actually changed you. Chances are, at some point, they told you something you didn't want to hear. Maybe they said you were being unfair. Maybe they pointed out a pattern you couldn't see. It stung. But you knew they said it because they cared, and so you trusted it.

Real love is willing to risk the moment for the sake of the person. A friend who only ever tells you what you want to hear is protecting the friendship. A friend who will occasionally tell you the truth is protecting *you.*

It works the other direction too. If you want to be that kind of friend, it will cost you a few uncomfortable conversations. Proverbs says it's worth it: "Better is open rebuke than hidden love" (27:5). Say it kindly, say it privately, say it prayerfully. But don't let someone you love walk toward a cliff because you didn't want things to get awkward.
The Friend Who Shows Up
Of course, friendship isn't only about challenge. Proverbs is just as clear about presence.

"A friend loves at all times, and a brother is born for a time of adversity" (17:17). *At all times.* Not just when it's convenient, not just when the invitation is fun. The real test of a friendship is what happens when life falls apart: the diagnosis, the divorce, the long season of grief. Who's still there on the hard days? Who shows up without being asked?

There's a story in the Gospels I love for this. Four men carried a paralyzed friend to Jesus, but the house was so crowded they couldn't get him through the door. So they climbed on the roof, tore open the ceiling, and lowered him down in front of everyone (Mark 2:1–12). Scripture says Jesus saw *their* faith. They didn't heal their friend. They couldn't. But they carried him to the One who could.
That's the kind of friend most of us want. It's also the kind most of us are called to be.
If You Feel Alone Right Now

I'd be remiss not to say something to the reader who finished this post feeling more lonely than inspired. Maybe there aren't five people to think of. Maybe there's one, or none. Maybe you've moved, or grown apart from people, or been burned.

Friendship is rarely instant. Most of the deepest ones are built slowly, through small consistent things: showing up, asking a second question, following up after a hard week. And you don't need five. You need one or two. If you're not sure where to start, a church, a small group, or a Bible study is often the most natural place to meet people who are walking in the same direction. Be willing to be the one who reaches out first. It's awkward almost every time, and it's almost always worth it.
And know that you aren't as alone as you feel.
The Friend Who Sticks Closer

Proverbs 18:24 holds a sentence that might be the most beautiful thing the book says about friendship: "One who has unreliable friends soon comes to ruin, but there is a friend who sticks closer than a brother."

The first half is honest about human friendship. Some friends will let us down, and we will let others down. We're all unreliable sometimes. But the second half points to someone beyond us. A friend who sticks closer than a brother.

Jesus says it Himself, and He means it literally. "I no longer call you servants... Instead, I have called you friends" (John 15:15). And then, as if to prove it, He adds: "Greater love has no one than this: to lay down one's life for one's friends" (John 15:13). Not just a friend who stays when it's easy. A friend who stayed when it cost Him everything.
He knows you completely, and He hasn't left. He tells you the truth without crushing you. He carries you when you can't walk. And He is, more than anyone, the one worth becoming like.
So look again at those five names. And ask who is making you more like Him. Be intentional about leaning toward them. And be that kind of friend yourself.

items: Looking at the five people closest to you, who is shaping you most, and in which direction? Do you leave their company more like Christ or less? What might need to change, whether that's spending more time with some people or setting healthier limits with others?

Who in your life is willing to tell you the truth, and are you willing to hear it? Is there a "wound from a friend" you've been resisting? On the flip side, is there someone you love who needs an honest, gentle word from you?
Who could you show up for this week? Think of someone going through a hard season. What is one practical way you could carry them, the way the four friends carried the paralyzed man to Jesus?

blocks.text: Lord Jesus, thank You for being the friend who sticks closer than a brother. Thank You for the people You've placed in my life, and forgive me for the times I've taken them for granted or let them lead me away from You. Give me wise friends, the courage to be honest with them in love, and the willingness to show up when it's hard. Make me the kind of friend who points others back to You. Amen.
